channel.title: Joe Grand
channel.description:
Hacking, electronics, and other projects featuring Joe Grand, a computer engineer, hardware hacker, and former member of L0pht Heavy Industries, sometimes known as Kingpin. 

BEWARE OF SCAMMERS AND IMPERSONATORS! I DO NOT RESPOND TO PUBLIC COMMENTS AND WILL NOT SEND ANY UNSOLICITED MESSAGES.

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: Human Password Generator
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This was the winning contest entry by the Greek Geeks. They created a Human Password Generator using the badge that tracked the motion of the LEDs via a webcam and performed a calculation of the motion hash-to-password on the badge's JM60 MCU. (Sorry, the audio is a bit messed up)

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: POV displaying "DC16 HACKER"
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry was a firmware hack to use persistence-of-vision (POV) to display "DC16 HACKER" on the LEDs.

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: IR distance increase & audio generation
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry, by Solder Guy, was a hardware hack to enhance the IR transmit/TV-B-Gone distance via multiple high-power IR LEDs. He also attempted audio generation in firmware via pulse-width modulation (PWM) and an external low-pass filter, but ran out of time and didn't get it completely working.

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: LED animations & high-level scripting
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry, by charliex, was a firmware hack containing a number of animation sequences for the 8 LEDs. He also created a high-level, Logo-style scripting language for LED patterns to make it easy for anyone to modify their badge.

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: PRNG w/ PWM dimming
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry was a firmware modification for a pseudorandom number generator (PNRG), displaying the bits on the 8 LEDs. Dimming of the LEDs was also enabled using pulse-width modulation (PWM).

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: Nikon camera remote control/trigger
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry was a firmware modification to change the IR transmit code to emulator a Nikon camera remote control/trigger. This remote control will remotely enable the shutter of Nikon D40, D40X, D70S, D50, 8400, 8800, F75, F65, F55, N65, N75, Nuvis S, and Lite Touch cameras. Good for legitimate use or mischief. :)

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: Real-time binary clock with IR time sync
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry was a firmware modification to turn the badge into a real-time binary clock displaying the time on the 8 LEDs. Time could be synchronized with another badge via infrared (IR) and could be set using the USB debug port and a PC terminal program.

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: Optical trojan/covert channel via LED
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry was created by the guys at University of Delaware's CVORG group (http://www.cvorg.ece.udel.edu/defcon-16). They modified the badge to leak information via the LEDs. Known as an "optical trojan" or "covert channel," the badge's LEDs are blinking at a very fast rate undetectable to the human eye and transmitting "HELLO DEFCON" in Morse Code. The optical transmission can be picked up with simple optical receiver circuitry connected to a PC.

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: Fiber optics + POV displaying "DEFCON"
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry was a firmware hack to use persistence-of-vision (POV) to display "DEFCON" on the LEDs. The entrant also modified their badge with fiber optics.

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: Cellular Automaton
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry was a firmware modification to create a Cellular Automaton with two models: Rule 30, random number generator, and Rule 110, Turing-complete "spaceship pattern." Submitted by Patrick Cruce and Michael McGraw-Herdeg. More details here: http://ssl.berkeley.edu/~pcruce/

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: Multicolor LEDs & IR distance hack
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry, by Unknown, is an LED pattern generator with added multicolor LEDs. Animation sequences include, but not limited to, Walking LEDs, Knight Rider, Reverse Knight Rider, Binary Counter, Pseudorandom, and Circular.

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: LED animations & music generator
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry consists of a firmware hack for a variety of LED animations (binary counter + police light bar emulation) and a music generator created with external hardware (Parallax BS2sx).

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: Camera shock and flash circuit addition
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This is a hardware addition of a camera flash charging/discharging circuit by Unknown.

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: Motion-generated/context-sensitive music
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry was a combination hardware/firmware hack and was the 3rd place winner in the contest. Motion-generated/context-sensitive music using an external accelerometer connected to the JM60 MCU. Also features "snooze alert" by making sound if a tilt is detected. (Sorry, the audio is crappy on this one)

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: Mac Front Row and HP Laptop 0wning
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This is the 2nd place contest entry by BonzoESC, Sterling, Critta, and Jymbolia. The hack uses the badge's IR transmitter to emulate Macintosh Front Row and HP Pavilion DV series laptop remote controls, allowing general mischief. Source code for the hack can be found here: http://github.com/bkerley/dc16_badge

videos.t: DC16 Badge Hack: TV-B-A.D.D.
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 16 Badge Hacking Contest. This entry by Major Malfunction replaces the TV-B-Gone (www.tvbgone.com) functionality of the badge with TV-B-A.D.D., which continuously changes the channel of any TV within its range.

videos.desc: From the DEFCON 15 Badge Hacking Contest. The winning contest entry by Team Osogato (Len Sassaman, Meredith Patterson, Dustin Cooper, Martin Murray, Tongen, and Maxinux). The two capacitive sensors are used to adjust the levels of the input signal and three shades of "greyscale" are used to create a fading effect on the display. videos.t: DC14 Badge Hack: Event Generator Ghoul (EGG)
videos.desc: From the DEFCON 14 Badge Hacking Contest. The winning Badge Hacking contest entry by Scott Scheferman (Shagghie) called the Event Generator Ghoul (EGG). Scott modified the LEDs on his badge to serve as event generators into his analog synthesizer. He connected the hacked badge to his Cwejman synthesizer's envelope generator and LPF cutoff frequency modulation jacks via a 1/4" stereo plug. He also installed two piezo buzzers/tweeters onto the badge to verify his initial concept and for debugging purposes. videos.t: RoboFlush: The Automatic Toilet Flusher

The arcade-style PC joystick uses two potentiometers (one for each axis) and had a number of buttons. The joystick was connected to a hacked Stelladaptor interface (Atari 2600-to-USB circuit) that connected to a PC laptop which controlled the Little RHex robot over a wireless interface. videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Wearable Airbag episode. This project was designed to prevent someone from serious injury at a fall of thirty feet. More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pt-wearable-airbag/

videos.t: Prototype This: Personal Airbag silly string/accelerometer test

The system is based on a DEFCON 15 badge, which has a Freescale QG8 microprocessor and MMA7260 accelerometer. When motion is detected in any of the three axis above a defined threshold, the solenoid is triggered and Silly String spews out. The can was almost empty by the time I took this video. videos.t: Prototype This: Magnetic sensor demonstration
videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Virtual Sea Adventure episode. Simple demonstration of the MLX90333 3-D Magnetic Joystick sensor. The oscilloscope is set to X/Y mode and the X- and Y-axis analog output voltages of the sensor are connected to the channel 1 and 2 inputs, respectively, of the scope. This device was ultimately used to control an ROV while being underwater. More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pt-virtual-sea-adventure/

videos.t: Prototype This: Magnetic sensor connected to an Etch-a-Sketch
videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Virtual Sea Adventure episode. This is a simple demonstration of using a Melexis MLX90333 3-D Joystick Position sensor to control the two axis of an Etch-a-Sketch. The sensor detects a position of a magnet over its face in X and Y dimensions. The analog output signals are fed through an A/D into a BASIC Stamp which sends the proper PWM pulses to the servos. This system was ultimately used in the build to control the ROV while under water. More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pt-virtual-sea-adventure/

videos.t: Prototype This: Traffic Busting Truck testing
videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Traffic Busting Truck episode. Testing our truck that can elevate itself, drive over traffic, move in any direction, and autonomously park. This video was the first time we had it up on its legs and we had no idea what would happen. More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pt-traffic-busting-truck/

videos.t: Prototype This: Omni-directional couch testing
videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Traffic Busting Truck episode. This was a test couch that we built to verify the functionality and control of the Airtrax omnidirectional (Mecanum) wheels. Control is achieved by a wireless Playstation 2 controller, its data being received by a BASIC Stamp and processed to send the required analog voltages to the Airtrax control box. More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pt-traffic-busting-truck/

videos.t: Prototype This: Couch surfing
videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Traffic Busting Truck episode. Surf's up for Zoz as he rides our omnidirectional couch. Control is achieved by a wireless Playstation 2 controller, its data being received by a BASIC Stamp and processed to send the required analog voltages to the Airtrax control box. More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pt-traffic-busting-truck/

videos.t: Prototype This: Autonomous parking couch
videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Traffic Busting Truck episode. This video shows our first successful test of the autonomous parking couch. The system uses Airtrax omnidirectional (Mecanum) wheels and a variety of sensors (ultrasonic, infrared, and stereo vision) to move forward along a length of cars until it detects a space large enough for it to slide into. Then, it moves sideways until it detects a curb (or, in our case, a piece of wood). There is absolutely no human interaction here at all. More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pt-traffic

videos.t: Prototype This: Waterslide Simulator testing
videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Backyard Waterslide Simulator episode. This video was taken during the many days of control system testing and tweaking of our 30-foot computer-controlled waterslide simulator. The system had a series of hydraulics to lift, tilt, and spin the simulator. I still can't believe it actually worked! More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pt-waterslide-simulator/

videos.t: Prototype This: The Pizza Pie Pack
videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Autonomous Pizza Delivery episode. Here's a short video I made showing the features of the Pizza Pie Pack (magnetic stripe reading, motor control, optical sensing) the night before our big payoff. Based on a Parallax BS2. More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pt-automated-pizza-delivery/

videos.t: Prototype This: Robo Dog Sitter testing
videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Robo Dog Sitter episode. This system is a fully autonomous robotic dog sitter complete with video conferencing capabilities, remote tug-o-war, ball fetch mechanism, and treat dispenser. It can remotely trigger a door to open, which is what we were testing here before the payoff. More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/prototype-this/

videos.t: Prototype This: Personal Airbag PCB fabrication
videos.desc: Behind the scenes of Discovery Channel's Prototype This from the Wearable Airbag episode. This is a video of fabricating the freefall detection circuit board of our project using the T-Tech Quickcircuit 5000 PCB prototyping machine. This video is at 20x speed. The actual board only took about 20 minutes to complete, which was a lifesaver in the "need it now" world of TV production. More info here: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pt-wearable-airbag/ and http://www.t-tech.com

videos.desc:

Further information about the module is available at http://www.parallax.com and http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/laser-range-finder/

videos.t: LRF: High-Speed Pulse Generator and Detector
videos.desc:
My experiments during the development of a low-cost Laser Range Finder module for Parallax. This video shows a high-speed pulse generator and detector that I was planning to use for a time-of-flight based ranging system. This approach was ultimately scrapped in favor of optical triangulation using a laser diode and CMOS camera. 

Further information about the final product is available at http://www.parallax.com and http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/laser-range-finder/

videos.t: Using Tribble to extract RAM from an active computer system
videos.desc:
Demonstration of extracting volatile memory from an active computer system using the proof-of-concept Tribble device. Tribble accesses the target's memory directly through DMA via the PCI bus and does not require any software or drivers to be loaded.

This project was originally developed by Joe Grand of Grand Idea Studio and Brian Carrier circa 2000-2003 and brought back to life in May 2012. More information on the project, including technical details, can be found at http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/tribble/

videos.t: PCB Solder Mask Removal: Abrasive Sand Blasting 2
videos.desc:
Raw video from our PCB Deconstruction Techniques research: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pcbdt/

Removing solder mask via abrasive sand blasting. TP Tools Skat Blast 1536 Champion blast cabinet with an 80 PSI (pounds per square inch), 10-15 CFM (cubic feet per minute) output of 60 grit aluminum oxide. Sand blasting and PCBs aren't usually mentioned in the same sentence, but the results were reasonably good, leaving only minor pitting of the underlying copper surface. This technique is not suitable for fine pitch, highly integrated PCBs.

Unsuccessful attempt at delayering a multi-layer printed circuit board via heat gun. Milwaukee MHT-750 with a maximum operating temperature of 1000 degrees F. Exposure to the heat gun eventually caused the PCB’s inter-layer adhesive to soften slightly, allowing us to attempt to peel layers apart. This method runs the risk of completely destroying the target PCB through excessive heat or physical force and is not practical for controlled delayering.

videos.desc:

Control and manipulation of milling, drilling, and routing procedures is achieved using T-Tech’s IsoPro software running on a host computer, except for tool type, tool cutting depth (Z-axis), and solenoid force, which are manually set.

videos.t: PCB Solder Mask Removal: Dremel Flapwheel
videos.desc:
Raw video from our PCB Deconstruction Techniques research: http://www.grandideastudio.com/portfolio/pcbdt/

We achieved moderate success at removing solder mask, though traces were still destroyed on a small section of the PCB. The tool was difficult to align and must be kept flat to prevent an edge from digging into the PCB.

The receiver circuitry is my open source OpticSpy Digital hardware, which receives the transmissions from the LED and converts them to a TTL-level signal suitable for connection to a PC.
